title: EBU (European Broadcasting Union), R 128: Loudness Normalisation and Permitted Maximum Level of Audio Signals
text:
## EBU R 128, the loudness normalisation standard

EBU R 128 is the recommendation from the European Broadcasting Union that shifted professional audio from peak based leveling to loudness based leveling. The core rule: normalise programmes to a Target Level of an average programme loudness of -23 LUFS (Loudness Units relative to Full Scale). This single number is the anchor every broadcaster and increasingly every streaming and podcast workflow measures against.

## The three descriptors

R 128 defines a programme by three measurable descriptors that must be reported together, not just a single loudness figure:

1. Programme Loudness, the integrated loudness of the whole programme, target -23 LUFS.
2. Loudness Range (LRA), a statistical descriptor of how much the loudness varies across the programme (measured per EBU Tech 3342).
3. Maximum True Peak Level, the highest true peak value reached, measured with a true peak meter to catch inter sample peaks that a normal sample peak meter misses.

## Why LUFS and not peak

Before R 128, engineers normalised to the highest sample peak, which does not reflect how loud a track actually sounds to a human. Two files can share the same peak level yet differ wildly in perceived loudness. R 128 instead uses the ITU-R BS.1770 loudness measurement algorithm (K-weighting plus gating) so the number tracks human perception. The unit LUFS is absolute (Full Scale reference); LU (Loudness Units) is the same scale used to express a difference or a relative offset. A change of 1 LU equals a change of 1 dB.

## Practical consequence

Because R 128 targets an average loudness rather than a peak, a compliant mix keeps natural dynamics: quiet passages stay quiet and loud passages stay loud, as long as the integrated average lands on -23 LUFS and the true peak stays under the permitted maximum. This is the opposite of squashing everything to the ceiling. The standard is maintained by the EBU and is paired with the metering spec EBU Tech 3341, the loudness range spec EBU Tech 3342, and the practical guidelines EBU Tech 3343.

title: Spotify for Artists, Loudness Normalization
text:
## Spotify loudness normalization

Spotify normalizes playback so tracks sound about equally loud regardless of how each was mastered. All tracks are adjusted to -14 dB LUFS as measured according to the ITU 1770 standard (integrated loudness across the whole track). Normalization happens at playback only: Spotify states we don't process or change your audio tracks before playback, so the stored master is untouched and the adjustment is a simple gain change applied to the listener's stream.

## True peak recommendation for masters

Spotify advises keeping the master's true peak below -1 dB TP (True Peak) max for lossy formats. If a master is mastered louder than -14 dB LUFS, Spotify recommends keeping the True Peak below -2 dB to prevent distortion introduced during transcoding to lossy codecs (inter sample peaks can push a lossy encoder into clipping even when the sample peak looked safe).

## How gain is applied

Negative gain is applied to masters louder than -14 dB LUFS, lowering the volume without adding distortion. Positive gain is applied to masters quieter than -14 dB LUFS; when boosting quiet tracks, the system leaves 1 dB headroom for lossy encodings and respects the track's own headroom limit so it will not push a quiet track into clipping.

## Listener volume settings (Premium)

Spotify offers three normalization targets the listener can choose:

- Loud: -11 dB LUFS, with a limiter engaged at -1 dB to prevent distortion.
- Normal: -14 dB LUFS (the default).
- Quiet: -19 dB LUFS.

These apply across all playback formats, including lossless. The key craft takeaway: because loud masters are simply turned down to -14 LUFS, mastering a track hotter than the target buys no loudness advantage on Spotify and only sacrifices dynamics and risks transcoding distortion.

title: Transom.org, The Audio Producer's Guide To Loudness
text:
## LUFS, LU, and true peak defined

LUFS stands for Loudness Units relative to Full Scale, the measurement unit for perceived loudness. LUFS values are negative numbers, and a value closer to zero is louder: -20 LUFS is louder than -24 LUFS. LU (Loudness Units) describe the relationship or difference between two measurements; a 4 LU difference is a clearly audible distinction. True Peak (dBTP) is a more accurate peak measurement that uses oversampling to catch inter sample peaks, and it is sometimes required by delivery standards.

## Momentary, short term, and integrated

Loudness meters report several time windows. Short Term is a rolling 3 second average that aligns well with the pacing of speech and is the primary reading to watch while mixing voice content. Momentary is a much shorter window. Integrated loudness measures the entire piece from start to finish and predicts consistency between episodes of a series, so it is the number that determines whether two episodes will match in perceived volume.

## Production target vs distribution target

For voice centric content the article recommends mixing to a production standard of -24 LUFS on the Short Term meter. That target leaves sufficient headroom and matches the ATSC A/85 standard and U.S. public radio (PRSS) requirements. For podcast distribution the common targets are -18 or -16 LUFS, which you reach by applying loudness normalization to the finished file. Crucially, normalizing the final file raises the whole mix uniformly without rebalancing the internal elements, so you do not re mix, you simply lift the integrated level to the distribution target.

## Practical loudness metering workflow

1. Install a loudness meter plug in on your master track.
2. Focus on the Short Term reading while mixing.
3. Target voices to -24 LUFS, accepting about plus or minus 1 LU variance.
4. Keep an eye on peak meters to prevent clipping.
5. Apply loudness normalization to the final mix if distribution requires a higher level such as -16 LUFS.

The guide's core lesson is that loudness (LUFS), not peak, is the correct target for consistent, comfortable listening, and that you separate the mixing target from the distribution target.

title: Transom.org, Podcasting Basics Part 3: Audio Levels and Processing
text:
## Target loudness for podcasts vs radio

The podcasting standard is -16 LUFS, versus the radio broadcast standard of -24 LUFS. Podcasts adopt the louder -16 LUFS target so episodes play back at a consistent, comfortable volume on phones and earbuds where the broadcast target would feel too quiet.

## Gentle per track compression

For compression on individual tracks the guidance is gentle: a ratio of 3:1 or 4:1, aiming for about 4 to 6 dB of gain reduction on the loud peaks. The intent is to even out level without audibly squashing the voice.

## Limiting on the master track

Put a limiter on the master track to control any stray peaks that could otherwise create distortion. Set the limiter threshold to -3 dB or less and the output level just below 0 dBFS, for example -0.5 dBFS or -1 dBFS. This catches occasional peaks without pumping the whole mix.

## EQ technique

Use a high pass filter to reduce low frequency rumbles, wind noise, and P pops. To fix a specific problem tone, use a parametric EQ: sweep the frequency up and down to find the offending area, then pull the line down to reduce the frequencies in that region. Be gentle, because dramatic EQ adjustments often sound unnatural.

## Noise reduction philosophy

The governing principle: it is always better to eliminate the noise before you record it, rather than counting on fixing it with software. Prevention at the source beats repair in post.

## Normalization and processing order

Traditional peak normalization is unreliable for matching perceived loudness; use loudness based normalization instead so episodes match a loudness standard consistently. The processing order is gentle compression per track, then limiting on the master track, then loudness normalization or export. Remember that adding EQ, compression, or effects changes the final output level, so keep watching the loudness meter on the master track as you work.

title: Transom.org, Podcasting Basics Part 5: Loudness for Podcasts vs. Radio
text:
## Two different loudness targets

Radio uses -24 LUFS and podcasts use -18 LUFS. These are deliberately different because the listening device and the listening environment are different. Radio playback runs through capable hardware in relatively controlled settings, so it can carry a wider dynamic range. Podcasts play on phones and tablets, which do not have the highest quality audio playback capabilities and struggle to amplify lower level content to a comfortable volume because of hardware constraints.

## Why the environment matters

Podcast listeners are usually on the go: commuting by subway or bus, walking, doing the dishes, or driving. Those environments are noisy, so the program has to sit louder to stay intelligible over the background. A -24 LUFS podcast would disappear under road noise.

## Dynamic range is the tradeoff

The -24 LUFS radio standard allows for a wider dynamic range, so producers can keep natural soft and loud passages. The higher -18 LUFS podcast target requires reducing dynamic range to reach that loudness without distortion. You cannot simply record hotter to get there: if you sat down with a portable recorder and a shotgun mic and tried to record your voice at the equivalent of -18 LUFS, you would distort the recorder.

## The correct workflow

Mix all production at -24 LUFS, then apply limiting and gain adjustment to reach -18 LUFS for podcast distribution. You do the creative mixing at the safe, headroom rich production level and only push to the loud distribution level as a final normalization step, so you never track or mix into distortion.

title: iZotope, RX 11 Documentation: Spectral De-noise
text:
## The two step Learn process

Spectral De-noise removes unwanted tonal and broadband noise by first learning a noise profile. Make a selection of the longest section of noise you can find in the file, ideally a few seconds in length, that contains only the noise and none of the content you want to keep, then activate Learn to establish the noise baseline. The module learns best from continuous, unchanging background noise such as steady hiss or air conditioning hum. If the background noise changes over time, a single learned profile will not track it well.

## Threshold and reduction

The Threshold parameter sets the signal to noise separation. Higher thresholds suppress more noise but risk removing quiet audio detail; lower settings preserve subtle components but may introduce unwanted modulation. The Reduction amount can be controlled separately for tonal noise (hum, buzz) and random noise (hiss), so you can target the specific noise character without over processing the rest.

## Avoiding musical noise artifacts

Over aggressive noise reduction produces musical noise, described as chirpy or watery sounds. RX offers multiple quality algorithms (A through D); higher qualities reduce these artifacts at the cost of more CPU. An artifact control slider balances a spectral subtraction approach against a wideband gating approach, letting you trade one kind of artifact for another to find the least objectionable result.

## Noise floor shaping

After denoising, residual noise remains at a calculated floor level, shown in yellow on the spectrum display. Synthesis, enhancement, masking, and whitening controls let you shape this remaining noise so it keeps the original character or takes on a neutral, less distracting character. The craft lesson: a small amount of natural residual noise usually sounds better than a heavily scrubbed, artifact ridden result, so reduce only as much as you need.

title: iZotope Learn, Dialogue Repair: 6 Problems You Thought You Couldn't Fix
text:
## Matching the RX module to the problem

Professional dialogue repair means picking the right specialized tool rather than blasting everything with one denoiser. RX exposes distinct modules, each aimed at a class of problem.

## The six problems and their modules

1. Intermittent noises like sirens, barks, and squeaks: use Spectral Repair in Attenuation mode. Isolate the offending frequencies in the spectrogram, and select the harmonics along with the fundamental so the whole anomaly is removed while the underlying speech is preserved.

2. Ambience gaps left after a repair: use Ambience Match. Its learn function samples the ambience of whatever you select, then fills the hole with matching room tone so the repair is inaudible rather than a dead silent gap.

3. Vocal distortion and clipping: combine De-clip, De-click, and De-crackle. Apply De-clip first to reconstruct clipped peaks, then use the gain tool to pull down visible distortion lines in the spectrogram, then De-click for thumps and De-crackle for high end artifacts.

4. Wind noise: use De-wind, a single module that minimizes wind rumble without layering spectral repair, denoising, and EQ.

5. Dynamic background noise under dialogue: use Dialogue Isolate to separate the voice from changing environmental sound such as machinery and traffic that a static noise profile cannot handle.

6. Blending looped or overdubbed dialogue (ADR) with location audio: use Dialogue Match to build a reference profile from the production sound and apply its acoustics and ambience to the studio recording in one step.

## The underlying principle

The expert move is diagnosis before treatment: identify what kind of defect you have (broadband hiss, a tonal hum, an intermittent event, clipping, reverb, changing background) and reach for the module built for it, in a sensible order, rather than over denoising and leaving watery artifacts.

title: iZotope Learn, Gain Staging: What It Is and How to Do It
text:
## What gain staging is

Gain staging is the process of making sure the audio is set to an optimal level for the next processor in the chain in order to minimize noise and distortion. Every stage of a signal path, the preamp, the channel, each plugin, the bus, and the master, has an ideal input level, and gain staging is the discipline of feeding each stage a healthy level rather than one that is too quiet (buried in the noise floor) or too hot (clipping the next stage).

## Headroom

Headroom is the buffer or safety zone in an audio signal that accommodates transient spikes and loud moments without causing distortion. In analog systems it is the room available before hitting the distortion point of the gear. In digital, the hard ceiling is 0 dBFS.

## Why levels must not hit 0 dBFS

Exceeding 0 dBFS (decibels relative to Full Scale) during export creates hard digital clipping that permanently damages the audio file. When exporting at 24-bit or lower, any distortion above this ceiling is irreversible, so the master bus output must remain below 0 dBFS.

## Recommended target levels

For individual tracks, aim for roughly -18 dBFS with the fader at unity, and some engineers target -20 dBFS for extra headroom. This mirrors the analog reference level (0 VU) and keeps plugins operating in their sweet spot rather than being slammed. The master bus output must stay below 0 dBFS.

## Noise floor and unity gain

The noise floor is the inherent, constant, audible hiss present in any recording. Good gain staging keeps the signal loud enough to sit above the noise floor while staying clear of distortion. Unity gain is the reference point where a fader sits at its neutral position (marked 0) and applies no level change, so you can set levels with input gain and trims rather than fighting the fader.

title: Sound on Sound, Gain Staging In Your DAW Software
text:
## 24-bit recording gives you enormous headroom

Modern DAW projects default to 24-bit recording, which offers substantially more dynamic range than most users need. As Sound on Sound puts it, digital recordings at 24-bit resolution offer a greater dynamic range than most users need, because the digital system's noise floor is so far below the wanted signal that you just don't need to think about it any more. A 24-bit system delivers an ample signal to noise ratio while leaving bags and bags of headroom.

## You no longer need to record hot

Maximizing recording levels was critical for 16-bit systems, but it is obsolete now. The old habit of tracking as hot as possible to beat the noise floor risks clipping the converter for no benefit on a 24-bit system.

## Recommended peak levels

Specific guidance: if you take the sound with the highest peak levels and set it so that it peaks at between -12 and -18 dBFS, you should not run into problems with plugins or summing on the mix bus. The author would not expect to see peaks on the channel meters reading more than -8 to -10 dBFS, and lower is often better.

## Why hot levels overdrive analog modeled gear

Professional converters output +24 dBu for a 0 dBFS signal, which is the clipping level of most analog gear. For engineers who mix hot, with average mix levels around -6 dBFS, the gear (and analog modeled plugins calibrated to that reference) is handling signals that are around 18 dB hotter than it was designed to cope with, which is why hot digital levels can sound harsh through analog style processors.

## The headroom margin

Keeping a 20 dB headroom margin in the DAW avoids that problem and will not compromise the digital noise floor, because that noise floor is still 95 dB lower. The lesson: give yourself generous headroom, target around -18 dBFS average, and stop chasing the ceiling.

title: iZotope Learn, Compression: When and How to Use It
text:
## The core compressor controls

A compressor reduces dynamic range by turning down signal that exceeds a set level. The five controls every editor must understand:

## Threshold

The level at which compression begins to engage. Signal below the threshold passes untouched; signal above it is reduced. Setting the threshold too low over compresses and can make a vocal sound squashed and lifeless.

## Ratio

Determines compression intensity, how much the signal above the threshold is turned down. A fixed ratio of 4:1 means for every 4 dB the input rises above threshold, the output rises only 1 dB. Higher ratios create more aggressive compression; a very high ratio approaches limiting.

## Attack

Controls how quickly compression responds once a signal exceeds the threshold. Attack shapes transient response. A medium to medium slow attack with a faster release emphasizes transients (lets the initial hit through before clamping down), while a relatively fast attack softens transients, for example taming the stick attack on overhead cymbals.

## Release

Determines how quickly compression stops after the signal drops below threshold. Use release to your advantage: a quicker release emphasizes each note, while a slower release smooths the sound and fits a bass into the drum's pocket. Too fast a release can cause audible pumping.

## Knee and makeup gain

The knee affects how strict the compression is around the threshold point: a hard knee clamps abruptly at the threshold, a soft knee eases compression in gradually for a more transparent sound. Because compression lowers overall level, makeup gain (output gain) restores the perceived loudness so you can A/B the compressed and uncompressed signal at matched volume, which is the only honest way to judge whether the compression helped.

title: iZotope Learn, 3 Uses for Parallel Compression in Audio Mastering
text:
## What parallel compression is

Parallel compression means blending a heavily compressed (or otherwise affected) signal with the dry, unprocessed one. Historically it was called New York Style compression after the mix engineers in New York City who popularized it. Because the untouched dry signal keeps the natural transients while the crushed signal fills in the low level detail, you gain density and punch without flattening the dynamics the way a single hard compressor would.

## How to route it

You need either a wet/dry control (labeled mix or parallel) built into the plugin, or a DAW routing with separate buses for the dry signal and the compressed signal blended together. Latency compensation must be enabled, otherwise the two paths drift out of phase and cancel.

## Settings for punch vs density

To add punch: use longer attack times (about 10 to 100 ms depending on the snap you want), a shorter release (around 100 ms), and a higher ratio (4:1). Let the transients pop through the dry path.

To add density: switch to a smoother mode with faster attack and release (attack under 10 ms, release under 50 ms) and a higher ratio (4.5:1 and up), which brings quiet details up without losing the transient.

## Blend level

Blend the compressed signal well below the dry signal, typically 14 to 22 dB lower, and use A/B comparison to find the sweet spot rather than over processing. Multiband parallel compression lets you enhance specific frequency ranges, and linear phase crossovers help avoid coloration. The point of the technique: keep the life of the original while adding weight underneath it.

title: iZotope Learn, 7 Tips for Using Subtractive EQ When Mixing Audio
text:
## Subtractive vs additive EQ

Subtractive EQ reduces a range to shape the sound, while additive EQ boosts a range. The pro default is to cut rather than boost, because cutting a competing frequency creates room in the mix instead of just making one element louder, and it avoids piling up energy near the ceiling.

## Boost first, then cut (the sweep technique)

If you are not sure which frequencies are causing a problem, find them with a big narrow boost: dial in a significant gain boost with a high Q, sweep it across the spectrum until the offending resonance jumps out, then pull that band down. This sweep and destroy method locates a resonance precisely before you cut it.

## Know your Q

Q sets the bandwidth of the band. A Q value around 1 is useful for broad unmasking and tonal shaping, while a value around 12 is better for surgically removing an annoying nasal resonance. Narrow Q for surgical resonance fixes, broad Q for gentle tone shaping.

## Solo to find resonances

Temporarily solo the instrument to isolate and audition specific frequencies, which makes a ringing resonance easier to pinpoint. Then unsolo and confirm the cut works in the full mix.

## Do not overdo cuts

Two cautions: the more you cut a range of frequencies, the less natural it sounds, so do not over cut the amplitude of a single band; and do not make too many cuts, because stacking many aggressive cuts can produce weird resonances that seem devoid of life. Make one cut, listen, and only add another if needed.

## Use dynamic EQ when static will not do

When a static cut removes too much (killing the frequency even when it is not offending), a dynamic EQ lets the content through normally and only cuts when the level in that band gets too high, which sounds more natural. A transparent, non saturating EQ is best for surgical cleanup where you do not want to add harmonic color.

title: iZotope Learn, What is De-essing? The Dos and Don'ts of Using a De-esser
text:
## What a de-esser is

A de-esser is a type of audio compressor that applies gain reduction to sibilance and other high frequency issues in a vocal track. Sibilance is the harsh sound produced when pronouncing letters like s, f, sh, and ch. Left unchecked it is fatiguing and can distort on cheap playback.

## Sibilance frequency range

Sibilant frequencies typically occur between 4 and 10 kHz, though they can extend as low as 1.5 to 2 kHz depending on the vocalist and microphone combination. The exact center varies per voice, so you tune the target frequency to the specific recording.

## How de-essers work

De-essers operate as frequency specific compressors: they detect an excessive level of sibilance in the target frequency range and reduce gain only in response to it, suppressing harshness while preserving intelligibility. Key parameters are the threshold (the level at which gain reduction begins), the amount and target frequency, and attack/release, which most modern de-essers automate to respond naturally to fast sibilant events.

## Approaches

Wideband reduces the entire signal when sibilance is detected (simple but can duck the whole vocal). Split-band applies compression only above a selected frequency cutoff, leaving the rest of the vocal untouched. Multiband targets multiple specific bands, and spectral de-essing uses narrow band compression across many frequencies for the most balanced, transparent result.

## Dos and don'ts

Do apply manual de-essing or clip gain reduction on the worst esses first to reduce how hard the processor has to work. Do use automation to adjust the de-esser per syllable. Do use multiple subtle de-essers rather than one aggressive one, which prevents the tell tale lisp that comes from over de-essing (removing so much high end that s turns into th). Consider where the de-esser sits relative to EQ and compression, since a bright EQ or a compressor can push sibilance back up. De-essing is not only for vocals: it also tames harsh guitars and cymbal heavy drum overheads.

title: DPA Microphones, Mic University: Proximity Effect in Microphones Explained
text:
## What causes the proximity effect

The proximity effect is the rise in low frequency response that happens as a directional microphone gets close to the source. It occurs exclusively in gradient (pressure gradient) microphones: cardioid, super cardioid, figure of eight, and similar patterns. A true omnidirectional (pressure) microphone does not exhibit it. Two mechanisms combine:

1. The primary gradient: sound reaches the diaphragm from both the front and a rear inlet. At low frequencies the wavelength is long, so the pressure difference across the 1 to 2 cm path is minimal; higher frequencies show greater differences.

2. The distance based gradient: when a point source is very close (about 1 m or less), an additional pressure difference appears. If a source is 2 cm from the front of the capsule and 4 cm from the rear, the sound pressure attenuates by 6 dB between the two positions, and this extra gradient boosts the low frequencies.

## How pattern and angle change it

The closer the directionality pattern comes to a figure of eight, the more proximity it exhibits; the proximity effect of a figure of eight microphone is much higher than a cardioid at 100 Hz. The effect is strongest on axis: if you turn the microphone off axis, the proximity effect is reduced.

## Distance and source type

How fast level (and the proximity buildup) changes with distance depends on the source: a point source drops 6 dB per doubling of distance, a line source 3 dB per doubling, and a plane source 0 dB. Practically, a vocalist singing 2 to 5 cm from a cardioid gets a strong bass lift that thins out by 20 to 30 cm.

## Using and controlling it

Proximity is a tool, not just a fault: a close vocalist gains warmth and authority (the classic radio voice), and you can ride the distance to add or remove body. To control unwanted boom, back off the mic, use a high pass filter, or choose a design like the DPA 4055 open cardioid (between wide and standard cardioid) that shows less proximity effect while keeping full low frequency response even at a distance.

title: iZotope, Digital Audio Basics: Sample Rate and Bit Depth
text:
## Sample rate and the Nyquist theorem

Sample rate is how many times per second an analog signal is measured. The governing rule is the Nyquist theorem: to record a frequency f, the sample rate must be at least 2 times f. Human hearing extends to roughly 20 kHz, so the minimum useful sample rate is about 40 kHz. A 44.1 kHz sample rate allows audio frequencies up to 22.05 kHz to be recorded (half the sample rate, the Nyquist frequency).

## Why 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz

The headroom above 20 kHz exists to prevent aliasing, a type of digital distortion that occurs when frequencies exceed the Nyquist frequency and fold back into the audible range. By placing the Nyquist frequency above human hearing, you can use gentler anti aliasing filters that do not color the audible band with steep filter artifacts. 44.1 kHz is the compact disc standard; 48 kHz is the video and broadcast standard, so if your work is going to video, record at 48 kHz from the start to avoid a conversion.

## Bit depth and dynamic range

Bit depth sets how many discrete amplitude values each sample can represent, which determines the noise floor and dynamic range. Each additional bit adds about 6.02 dB of dynamic range. 16-bit gives 65,536 possible values and about 96 dB of dynamic range (noise floor near -96.3 dBFS). 24-bit gives 16,777,216 values and about 144 dB of dynamic range (noise floor near -144.5 dBFS).

## Recommended settings

For most projects, 48 kHz (or 96 kHz) at 24-bit is a great choice: 24-bit gives so much dynamic range and such a low noise floor that you can record with generous headroom without worrying about hiss. The practical takeaway: record at 24-bit for the huge dynamic range, pick 44.1 or 48 kHz to match your delivery target, and do not assume ultra high sample rates audibly improve a finished mix, since their extra bandwidth sits entirely above human hearing.

title: Fora Soft, Loudness Normalization: EBU R128, ITU-R BS.1770, ATSC A/85
text:
## The ITU-R BS.1770 four step measurement pipeline

Almost every loudness rule in the world is built on ITU-R BS.1770, which defines how loudness is measured in four steps.

## Step 1, K-weighting

The algorithm applies a fixed pair of filters, together called K-weighting, that boost the frequencies the ear is sensitive to and trim the ones it is not. This is a high shelf pre filter that approximates the acoustic effect of the head, followed by a high pass (RLB) that rolls off the lowest frequencies. It aligns the digital measurement with human perception.

## Step 2, mean square energy

The algorithm squares every sample first. Squaring makes every value positive and corresponds to the signal's power, the rate at which it delivers energy. These squared values are then averaged to a perceptual energy figure.

## Step 3, gating

The signal is analyzed in 400 millisecond blocks, each overlapping the next by 75%. Two gates then discard blocks that would drag the average down unfairly: an absolute gate discards blocks quieter than -70 LUFS, and a relative gate removes blocks more than 10 LU below the first (ungated) average. Only the surviving blocks are averaged to produce the integrated loudness. Gating is what lets a program keep quiet passages and silence without lowering its measured loudness.

## Step 4, true peak

True peak (dBTP) is computed by oversampling the signal, reconstructing the waveform at four times the sample rate, so inter sample peaks that sit between the original samples are caught. A regular sample peak meter misses these.

## Regional targets built on BS.1770

EBU R128 targets -23 LUFS with a maximum true peak of -1 dBTP, measured over the whole programme, and allows a tolerance of about plus or minus 0.5 LU for file based content. ATSC A/85 (used in North American broadcast, enforced by the US CALM Act for commercials) targets -24 LKFS using a Dialogue Anchor Element approach and recommends a -2 dBTP peak ceiling. LKFS (Loudness, K-weighted, relative to Full Scale) and LUFS are the same unit, and a 1 dB change equals a 1 LU change.

title: Sound on Sound, The End Of The Loudness War?
text:
## What the loudness war is (the anti-pattern)

The loudness war is the decades long practice of competing to make one record sound louder than others, traced to a 1950s observation that louder jukebox records got played more. Digital removed vinyl's physical loudness limit, so engineers pushed further with heavy limiting and compression, often combined with spectral shaping, to increase the average energy level and minimise the crest factor (the gap between peak and average). The bitter irony: the audio format that offered the greatest dynamic range potential ever made available to the consumer is now routinely used to store music deliberately processed with the least possible dynamic range.

## Why louder is not better

Loudness perception depends on average energy, not peaks. Peak normalisation, raising the level so peaks hit a defined maximum, does not make a dynamic track sound as loud as a hyper compressed one at the same peak. But hyper compressed material sounds flat, lifeless and even boring compared with tracks that retain some musical dynamics. Bob Katz's phrase is that you want music that breathes; a continuous wall of sound is fatiguing.

## How loudness normalization ends the war

Streaming services apply automatic loudness matching, so a hyper compressed master is simply turned down to the platform target and gains nothing. Spotify has used a form of loudness normalisation from the day it launched. When everything is normalized to a standard such as -23 LUFS (HDTV) or around -16.5 LUFS (iTunes Sound Check), very heavily compressed music ends up sounding dull and feeble compared with more naturally dynamic material.

## The measurement proof

Comparing two commercial tracks normalized to -23 LUFS: a dynamic 1980s recording needed minimal adjustment and preserved transient peaks at about -4.5 dBTP, while a heavily remastered modern track, after being turned down to match loudness, reached only about -13.7 dBTP, losing roughly 9 dB of peak impact. The originally quieter, more dynamic track sounded more interesting and musical once normalization flattened the hyper compressed version. The lesson for an editor: in a loudness normalized world, preserve dynamics and hit the target loudness, do not crush the master chasing volume.

title: GIK Acoustics, Knowledge Base: Sound Proofing vs. Acoustics Treatment
text:
## Two different problems

Soundproofing and acoustic treatment are not the same thing, and confusing them wastes money. Acoustic treatment addresses how sound behaves inside a room. Soundproofing addresses stopping sound from passing between two spaces. GIK, an acoustic treatments company, notes it constantly fields soundproofing questions because so many people conflate the two.

## What acoustic treatment does

Acoustic treatment manages the reflections and reverberation inside the space to give a truer, clearer sound. The main tools are absorptive acoustic panels placed at first reflection points to tame slap echo and flutter, bass traps in the corners to control low frequency buildup, room modes, and standing waves, and diffusers to scatter sound and keep a room from sounding dead. For a voice recording space this is what removes the boxy, echoey room signature that a microphone would otherwise bake into every take.

## What soundproofing does

Soundproofing prevents sound transmission between rooms and requires mass, airtightness, and decoupling (isolation), for example added dense layers, sealed gaps, and structural separation so vibration does not carry through. It is a construction problem, not a panel you hang.

## The key misconception

Absorptive treatments do not soundproof a room. Foam panels, fiberglass traps, and acoustic curtains control reflections inside a space but do little to stop sound traveling through walls, ceilings, or doors. The diagnostic rule: if the problem is loud sound entering or leaving the room, it is a soundproofing issue; if the problem is echo, speech clarity, or a room that sounds bad, it is an acoustic treatment issue. For most editors, treating the first reflection points and corners is the single highest value change to recorded voice quality.

title: Production Expert, 5 More Common Audio Myths Debunked
text:
## Myth 1: Fix it in the mix

The myth claims deficiencies in performance or capture can be repaired later with DAW tools and plugins, so quality at the recording stage does not matter. The correction: a great performance with an issue can be salvaged, but an indifferent one will always be indifferent. Mixing enhances what you captured; it cannot manufacture a good performance or undo a fundamentally bad recording. Capture it right at the source.

## Myth 2: You need expensive professional plugins

The belief that a professional mix requires premium plugins. A blind test with a Grammy winning engineer found the only difference noted was that the stock reverb did not sound quite as good as the premium offering; apart from that the differences were insignificant. Stock plugins are capable; skill matters more than the brand.

## Myth 3: Phantom power damages ribbon mics

The myth that phantom power cannot be used safely with ribbon microphones. A modern ribbon mic is fine with phantom power, though sensible precautions like not hot plugging still apply.

## Myth 4: Different DAWs sound different

The claim that different DAW audio engines have an inherent tonal character. Null testing with polarity inversion finds no significant difference between most DAWs summing the same audio.

## Myth 5: Analog summing is inherently superior

The belief that mixing through an analog console beats digital summing. Testing showed there is nothing to call between the two versions of a mix. The through line of all five: chase capture quality and craft, not gear folklore.

title: iZotope Learn, Reflecting on Reverb: What It Is and How to Use It
text:
## What reverb is

Reverb happens when a sound occurs in a space and sends sound waves out in all directions; those waves reflect off surfaces and decay in amplitude until the reflections die off. Reverb is the sum of the direct sound, the early reflections, and the dense reverb tail.

## The key controls

Wet/dry balance sets how much processed (wet) reverb sits against the original (dry) signal. Pre-delay is the time gap between the direct sound and the start of the early reflections; a longer pre-delay keeps a voice clear and up front because the tail arrives after the word, preserving intelligibility. Decay time, also called RT60, is the time it takes for the sound pressure level in a space to fall by 60 dB; larger and more reflective rooms (concrete, hardwood) have longer decay times than small absorptive rooms (carpet). Damping controls high frequency absorption in the tail, so lower damping is brighter and higher damping is darker. Diffusion sets the dispersion and density of the reflections.

## Reverb types

Algorithmic reverb simulates the space through mathematical calculation, is flexible, and uses less CPU. Convolution reverb uses an impulse response captured from a real space or unit, sounds more realistic, and costs more CPU. Hall, room, and chamber emulate natural three dimensional spaces; plate and spring reverbs have a distinct two dimensional character from their mechanical origins.

## Using reverb without mud

Run reverb on a return channel at 100% wet and process it independently. To keep the mix clear, roll off the reverb return under about 200 Hz and above about 8 kHz so the tail does not add low mud or harsh top. For dialogue and voiceover, use pre-delay for clarity, keep the wet level modest, and if the source already has unwanted room, reach for de-reverb, gating, and EQ rather than adding more reverb on top.

title: Sound on Sound, Podcast Dialogue Editing
text:
## Two categories of work

Podcast production splits into audio sweetening (EQ and compression to shape tone) and detailed editing (removing unwanted sections and reducing distracting noises). The editing is where a raw conversation becomes a tight, listenable program.

## Removing ums, ers, and flubs

To remove filler words, ums, ers, and flubbed takes, select the offending range and cut it so the remaining audio closes the gap. Keep auto fades switched on: every time you cut audio this way a short fade out and fade in is applied at the edit point, which prevents the clicks and pops that hard cuts create. Crossfades at edit points are what make dialogue edits inaudible.

## Handling breaths

Do not simply delete every breath. Deleting them can sound unnatural, and reducing their volume so they are less prominent often gives a better result. A practical method is to split the breath into its own event and lower it in small steps, around 1 dB at a time, with crossfades to the adjacent audio, until it sits back without disappearing. A breath removed entirely can make the following word feel slammed in.

## Pacing and natural sound

The goal is natural pacing: tighten dead air and remove distractions, but keep the human rhythm. Over tightening every pause and breath makes an articulate speaker sound anxious or robotic, so leave some breaths and micro pauses in. Match your cuts to the speaker's cadence.

## Efficiency

Because this work is highly repetitive, build macros (single keystroke sequences) for the common moves like cut and close gap or reduce breath, so editing a long episode stays fast and consistent.

title: iZotope, What Is a True Peak Limiter?
text:
## Clipping and the true peak problem (anti-pattern)

Clipping is what happens when a signal exceeds 0 dBFS: the waveform's rounded peak gets shaved flat and the flat top is audible distortion. A true peak limiter is a brick wall limiter that uses oversampling to more accurately follow and control peak levels, preventing the output from exceeding 0 dBFS by looking at the actual analog waveform between the digital samples.

## True peaks vs sample peaks

A standard digital meter shows sample peak levels, the highest value among the discrete samples. But the actual analog voltage that comes out of a digital to analog converter can be higher than the sample values on either side of it. These hidden maxima are inter sample peaks, or true peaks. The article shows an extreme example where the samples read -4 dBFS while the reconstructed analog waveform peaked at -1 dBTP, a 3 dB difference, and notes more extreme cases can exceed 7 dB. This is why a mix that looks safe on a normal peak meter can still clip a converter or a codec.

## Oversampling detection

True peak limiters catch these by oversampling: the sampling frequency is increased by a factor of at least four, generating extra sample points that track the analog signal between the original samples so the limiter can clamp the real peak.

## Lossy codec clipping risk

When audio exceeds 0 dBFS, lossy formats (MP3, AAC, and streaming services like Spotify) can introduce baked in clipping during encoding, distortion the listener cannot avoid by turning down. This is the concrete reason to leave true peak headroom.

## Recommended ceiling

The recommended true peak ceiling is around -1 to -0.3 dBTP depending on genre, balancing DAC reliability against practical listening. The safe default many standards and platforms use is -1 dBTP. The anti-pattern to avoid: mastering to 0 dBFS on a sample peak meter and assuming you are safe, then shipping a file that clips on lossy playback.

title: Shure, How to Record and Mix Vocals
text:
## Microphone distance

For most singers, position the microphone about 10 to 20 centimeters (4 to 8 inches) from the mouth. The single most important rule is to keep the distance constant throughout the performance, because any change in position drastically affects tone, level, and balance, which is hard to fix later.

## Polar pattern choice

Cardioid microphones are the standard for vocal recording: they capture sound primarily from the front (on axis) and reject sound from the rear (off axis), which reduces room ambience and increases isolation. The tradeoff is the proximity effect, where low frequencies become more pronounced as the vocalist moves closer. Omnidirectional microphones capture sound equally from all directions for a more open, natural sound, but they also pick up more room reflections, so they only work well in an acoustically good space. For most people it is safer to record with a directional mic (cardioid or hypercardioid) and add ambience artificially at mixdown.

## Microphone type

Large diaphragm condensers dominate studio vocal recording for their detail and tonal character, but expensive does not necessarily mean better: choosing a mic that complements the specific voice matters most. Dynamic (moving coil) microphones suit aggressive genres like rock, metal, and rap where a controlled, focused sound beats the extra detail of a condenser, and they are the rugged choice for live use.

## Pop filter and sibilance

A pop filter reduces the plosive bursts of air from P and B consonants and also helps keep the mouth to mic distance constant. To reduce sibilance, positioning the microphone slightly below direct mouth alignment (off the direct blast of the esses) helps without affecting the performance. The through line: capture a clean, consistent, well isolated voice at the source so post production is sweetening rather than rescue.
